title: A driver is buzzing, harassing or following you
summary: Don't engage. Get somewhere lit, open and busy, and call 911 if you feel threatened or are being followed.
steps: Do not react, gesture, or confront the driver. Retaliating escalates things.
Head to the nearest lit, open business or busy place with people.
If followed, do not go home. Go to a police station or open business.
If you feel threatened or are followed, call 911 now.
Tell dispatch your exact location and direction of travel.
If safe, note plate, make, model and color of the vehicle.
After you are safe, tap Close call to log the spot.
warnings: Never chase or block the vehicle to get a plate. Your safety comes first.
Apple Valley is patrolled by the San Bernardino County Sheriff, Apple Valley Patrol Station.
prevent: Plan night routes past open businesses so you always know the nearest safe place.

sources.org: California Highway Patrol (Sgt. Brian Pennings, via ABC30 Fresno 'Know the Road', Apr 30 2021)

title: Report a dangerous or harassing driver afterward
summary: If no one is in danger now, report the driver to the Sheriff's non-emergency line. Emergencies always go to 911.
steps: If anyone is in danger right now, call 911 instead.
Call the Sheriff's Desert non-emergency dispatch: (760) 956-5001.
Or call the Apple Valley Patrol Station: (760) 240-7400, open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Station address: 14931 Dale Evans Parkway, Apple Valley, CA 92307.
Give date, time, exact spot, what happened, and any plate or vehicle details.
Ask for a report or incident number and write it down.
Save any video or photos. Do not post the plate publicly.
warnings: The station office line is staffed business hours only; after hours use dispatch or 911.
The Sheriff page lists the Desert line without naming towns; Apple Valley is in the High Desert.

title: California's 3-foot passing law
summary: Drivers passing a bicycle must leave at least three feet. If they can't, they must slow down and pass only when it won't endanger you (VC 21760).
steps: Drivers may not pass a bicycle with less than three feet of clearance.
If another same-direction lane is open, drivers must change lanes to pass when practical and lawful.
If three feet isn't possible, drivers must slow and pass only when safe for you.
Violation is an infraction: $35 base fine, or $220 if a crash injures the cyclist.
Log the close pass with Close call; report it to the Sheriff if needed.
warnings: Knowing the law does not stop a close pass. Ride defensively and keep an escape space.
prevent: Use lights and leg reflectors so drivers spot you sooner and have time to move over.

sources.org: California Legislature (text via California Public Law)
sources.title: Vehicle Code 21760 (Three Feet for Safety Act)

qa.notes: Matches current VC 21760. Clarified lane-change wording and that $35/$220 are base fines; $220 applies when a collision injures the rider.

title: Required bike lights and reflectors at night
summary: Riding in darkness in California requires a white front light, a red rear reflector or light, and pedal and side reflectors (VC 21201).
steps: Front: white light visible from 300 feet ahead and to the sides.
A white light worn on your body may replace the bike-mounted front light.
Rear: red reflector, or solid or flashing red light with built-in reflector, visible 500 feet.
Pedals, shoes or ankles: white or yellow reflectors visible front and rear from 200 feet.
Sides: reflectors on each side, or reflective tires front and rear.
E-bikes: the rear red reflector or light rule applies at all hours, day too.
warnings: The rule covers roads, bikeways, and sidewalks where riding is allowed.
These are legal minimums. In one study, lights alone didn't help drivers recognize riders sooner.
prevent: Check light batteries before every night ride.

title: Where you can ride and when you can take the lane
summary: Slower riders keep as far right as practicable, but the law lets you move left for hazards, turns, passing, and lanes too narrow to share (VC 21202).
steps: Ride in the same direction as traffic.
If slower than traffic, ride as far right as practicable.
You may move left to pass, prepare a left turn, or avoid hazards.
Hazards include objects, parked or moving vehicles, people, animals, and surface problems.
If a lane is too narrow to share side by side, you may use the lane.
You may also move left when approaching a spot where you will turn right.
On one-way roads with two or more lanes, you may ride near the left edge.
warnings: On a two-lane road, if five or more vehicles line up behind you, pull off where safe (VC 21656).
Taking the lane is legal when conditions allow it, but some drivers still react badly. Stay calm, don't engage.

title: Can I ride on the sidewalk?
summary: California lets cities and counties regulate riding on sidewalks, so it depends on where you are. NIGHTRIDE has not confirmed Apple Valley's rule.
steps: State law lets local ordinances regulate bike riding on sidewalks.
Check the Town of Apple Valley code or call the Town at (760) 240-7000.
Where allowed, ride slowly and yield to people walking.
At night on a sidewalk, you still need lights and reflectors.
warnings: NIGHTRIDE could not confirm Apple Valley's specific sidewalk ordinance. Do not assume it is allowed.

title: Walking where there is no sidewalk
summary: Outside business and residence districts, walk near the left edge of the road, facing oncoming traffic (VC 21956).
steps: Use a sidewalk whenever one exists.
Outside business or residence districts, walk near the left edge, facing oncoming traffic.
You may use the right edge if no safe crossing exists or crossing is unsafe.
Wear bright clothes and carry a flashlight at night.
Never assume a driver sees you.
warnings: Drivers must use due care for you, and you must use due care too.
prevent: Carry a small flashlight on every night walk.

title: Walking home safely at night
summary: Be visible, stay alert, and pick lit routes. If someone follows you, change direction toward light and people.
steps: Plan your route on well-lit streets.
Wear bright clothes and carry a flashlight.
Keep your phone down when crossing streets.
Cross at crosswalks or intersections. Look left, right, then left again.
Watch for cars turning into your path.
If followed on foot, cross the street and go to a lit, populated place.
If you feel in danger, call 911.
warnings: Don't assume drivers can see you. Make eye contact with drivers before you cross.
prevent: Share your route and arrival time with someone before you leave.

title: You were just hit or crashed
summary: Call 911 first if anyone is hurt. Get out of traffic only if you safely can. Gather details once you are safe.
steps: Call 911 right away if anyone is hurt, including you.
If you are hurt, tell the 911 dispatcher and follow their instructions.
If no one is hurt, move out of traffic, then call 911.
Tell dispatch your location and if the driver left.
When safe, photograph the scene, vehicle, plate, and your bike.
Ask witnesses for names and phone numbers.
Ask the driver for name, address, license, insurance, plate, and owner info.
Ask the deputy or officer for the report number before leaving.
warnings: NIGHTRIDE does not give medical advice. If you are injured, call 911.

sources.title: California Driver's Handbook: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions

title: The driver hit me and left (hit-and-run)
summary: A driver in a crash that injures someone must stop, give their information, and help. Leaving is a crime (VC 20001, 20003).
steps: Call 911 now. Say the driver left and which way they went.
Give any plate, make, model, color, or damage you saw.
Do not chase the vehicle.
Ask nearby people if they saw it or have video.
Ask deputies for a report number.
warnings: NIGHTRIDE is not legal advice. For claims or charges, talk to a lawyer.

title: Get a copy of your crash or incident report
summary: Request Sheriff reports online, in person, or by mail. Crash victims and involved parties can usually get them.
steps: Keep your report number from the scene.
Request online through the county's public records portal (NextRequest).
Or go to your local Sheriff station, weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Bring photo ID.
Or mail: Sheriff's Records Division, PO Box 569, San Bernardino, CA 92402.
Expect a decision on release within 10 days; it can be extended.
Crashes on freeways or unincorporated county roads go through CHP. Request from CHP instead.
warnings: Parts of reports involving a crime or death may not be released right away.

title: What actually helps drivers see you
summary: Reflective strips on ankles and knees, which move as you pedal or walk, help drivers recognize you much sooner than vests or lights alone.
steps: Put reflective bands on both ankles. Ankles help most.
Add reflective bands at the knees if you can.
A reflective vest alone helps less than moving leg reflectors.
A fluorescent vest without reflective material does little at night.
Keep using legal lights; add leg reflectors on top of them.
warnings: In one closed-road study, bike lights alone did not make riders easier to recognize.
prevent: Leave reflective ankle bands clipped to your bike so you never ride without them.

sources.org: Accident Analysis & Prevention (Wood, Tyrrell et al., 2012)

sources.supports: Vest plus ankle and knee reflectors recognized at longer distances than vest or black clothing; static or flashing light did not improve conspicuity

sources.supports: Joint markings help pedestrians too (up to 3x recognition distance vs vest); cyclists wrongly believe a non-reflective fluorescent vest helps at night

qa.notes: Findings confirmed in both peer-reviewed abstracts and QUT page; narrowed 'fluorescent colors' to the fluorescent vest the research actually tested.

title: Where to mount your front light
summary: In a small closed-road study, drivers recognized riders sooner with a helmet-mounted white light than a handlebar light, especially with ankle reflectors.
steps: Keep the legal white front light on the bike or your body.
Consider a helmet-mounted white light as well.
Pair it with reflective ankle bands for the biggest benefit.
warnings: Based on one study of 15 young drivers on a closed road.
NIGHTRIDE found no research source on bike light aim or glare; we can't advise on angle.

title: Why night is more dangerous
summary: Riders and walkers face more risk in low light, and cyclists tend to think they are more visible than they really are.
steps: Assume drivers see you later than you think.
Ride and walk as if unseen until a driver clearly reacts.
Use lights, leg reflectors, and bright clothing every night trip.
prevent: Pick routes with streetlights when you have a choice.

title: Why your Close call reports matter
summary: Official crash records miss many bike incidents. Near-miss reports show danger spots before someone gets hurt.
steps: Tap Close call as soon as you are safe.
Add what happened in a few words: close pass, cut off, followed.
Report road hazards to the Town too, using Apple Valley Connect.
warnings: Close call reports are not police reports. For threats or crimes, call the Sheriff or 911.

title: Goatheads (puncturevine) and flat tires
summary: Puncturevine burs are hard and spiny and can puncture bike tires. The plant grows in low mats along roadsides in hot, dry weather.
steps: Watch for low mats with small yellow five-petal flowers along road edges.
Avoid riding through roadside dirt and weed mats when you can.
If you get a flat, move well off the road before fixing it.
Burs stick to tires and shoes. Remove them so you don't spread the plant.
warnings: Burs can also hurt people and pets who step on them.
prevent: Carry a spare tube or patch kit and a pump on every ride.

sources.org: UC Statewide IPM Program (UC Agriculture and Natural Resources)

title: Riding or walking in desert heat
summary: Plan trips for the coolest part of the day, carry water, and take shade breaks. If someone may have heat stroke, call 911.
steps: Travel in the coolest part of the day when you can.
Carry water and drink throughout the trip.
Take breaks in shade.
Know warning signs: cramps, heavy sweating, dizziness, headache, weakness, nausea.
Confusion, slurred speech, hot red skin, or fainting can mean heat stroke.
If someone may have heat stroke, call 911 right away.
warnings: NIGHTRIDE does not give medical advice. For heat illness, call 911 or seek medical care.
prevent: Check the forecast before longer trips.

title: Cold desert nights
summary: Wind makes cold more dangerous. Dress in layers, cover skin, stay dry, and get out of the wind.
steps: Wear several loose layers and cover exposed skin.
Protect ears, nose, fingers and toes. Mittens are warmer than gloves.
Stay dry. Change wet clothes once inside.
If stuck, shelter out of the wind.
If someone is confused, sluggish, or very cold, call 911.
warnings: NIGHTRIDE does not give medical advice. For cold injury, call 911.
prevent: Pack a warm layer even if it was hot when you left.

title: Strong wind or blowing dust
summary: High Desert gusts and dust can push you around and hide you from drivers. Check NWS alerts and shelter when it gets bad.
steps: Check the NWS San Diego forecast for 'Apple and Lucerne Valleys' before leaving.
Wind Advisory: secure loose items and travel with caution.
High Wind Warning: seek shelter in a sturdy building.
Dust Storm Warning means visibility half a mile or less. Get indoors if you can.
Without shelter, stay away from trees, power lines, and the roadside.
Treat downed power lines as live. Stay away.
Give trucks and trailers extra room; gusts can tip them over.
warnings: In dust, drivers may not see you even with lights.
prevent: If a High Wind or Dust Storm Warning is out, skip the trip or get a ride.
